notes: The pinned Greek names Asaph and Amos; these are not silently changed to Asa and Amon to match other genealogies.
“From whom” is feminine singular in Greek, referring to Mary. The pattern of fathers begetting sons changes at this point.
“Until” states what happened before the birth; this wording alone does not specify what happened afterward.
vocabulary: Messiah
The anointed one; this translates Greek Christos as a title rather than treating Christ as a surname.
Jesus
The name is linked in the verse to saving his people from their sins.

notes: The visitors are magi; the passage does not call them kings or give their number. “At its rising” can also be read “in the east.”
The victims are boys aged two and under. The violence and the scope Herod orders remain explicit.
Matthew speaks of the prophets in the plural and does not identify a single quotation source here.
vocabulary: Magi
Learned interpreters of signs, including heavenly phenomena, from the east.
Myrrh
An aromatic substance named with gold and frankincense among the gifts.

notes: Matthew’s Greek says carrying the sandals; the draft does not replace it with untying them from another account.
The voice’s “my Son” and the Spirit’s descent are retained without adding an explanation of the scene’s mechanics.
vocabulary: Repent
Turn from wrongdoing toward God; the proclamation joins this turning to the kingdom’s nearness.
Winnowing fork
An implement for separating grain from chaff, used in the judgment image.

notes: The verb can mean test or tempt. The narrative identifies the devil as the tester and retains the conditional “if you are God’s Son.”
“Handed over” recurs in Matthew for arrest, betrayal, and delivery into another’s power.
vocabulary: Word
The quotation treats life as dependent on what comes from God’s mouth, not bread alone.
Fishers of people
The calling keeps the fishermen’s work as its image.

notes: The pinned text does not qualify anger with “without cause.” Raca is an insult; Gehenna is the named judgment image.

The eye and hand sayings use graphic hyperbole about removing causes of sin, not medical instructions. “Sexual immorality” renders porneia, whose exact scope in the divorce saying is disputed; the passive wording about the woman is preserved.
“Evil” may also mean “the evil one.” “Complete” renders teleios and connects the command with the preceding call to undivided love.
vocabulary: Blessed
A declaration of favored standing, which can coexist with present mourning or persecution.
Gehenna
A term associated with judgment, distinct from Hades, the realm of the dead.
Quadrans
A small Roman copper coin; the saying presses repayment down to the last coin.

notes: The pinned text says righteousness, introducing the acts of giving, praying, and fasting that follow.

The unusual bread adjective can mean daily, needed for the day, or for the coming day. The forgiveness clause says “have forgiven.” The final petition can refer to evil or the evil one; the familiar closing doxology is not printed in this source.
A sound or single eye can carry a sense of generosity. The cubit saying may concern lifespan or stature; the measurement image remains. The pinned verse 33 does not add “of God” after kingdom.
vocabulary: Debts
The prayer’s image for what requires forgiveness; verses 14–15 speak directly of offenses.
Mammon
Wealth personified as a competing master.
Gentiles
People who are not Jewish; this identifies the comparison group within Jesus’ Jewish setting.

notes: The judgment warning develops through reciprocal measure and the log/speck image; the imagery remains concrete.
The contrast is between claims made in Jesus’ name and doing the Father’s will. The reported claims are not automatically endorsed by the narrator.
vocabulary: Holy; pearls
Valuable things in a deliberately sharp animal comparison.
Authority
The closing reaction concerns how Jesus teaches, in contrast to their scribes.

notes: The skin-disease term is broader than a modern diagnosis of leprosy. Pais can mean child or servant; servant fits this setting. Jesus’ reply in verse 7 can also be punctuated as a question: “Am I to come and heal him?”
The doubled “dead” saying is left sharp without inventing the father’s circumstances. Matthew names two men and the Gadarenes; these are not harmonized to other accounts.
vocabulary: Centurion
An officer in a military unit conventionally associated with a hundred soldiers.
Son of Man
Jesus’ recurring self-designation; its meaning develops across suffering, authority, and coming judgment.

notes: Verse 8 speaks of authority given to human beings in the plural. In verse 18 the ruler says his daughter has just died; this sequence is preserved.
The pinned verse ends with calling sinners; it does not add “to repentance.”
vocabulary: Tax collector
A person collecting revenue; the occupation is part of the social dispute over Jesus’ table companions.
Wineskins
Skin containers whose condition matters in the image of fermenting new wine.

notes: Simon’s designation concerns zeal, not Canaanite ancestry. The equipment restrictions follow Matthew’s wording, including the staff.

The timing of the Son of Man’s coming is not resolved in translation. Soul and body remain distinct in verse 28. “Apart from your Father” does not specify whether knowledge, permission, or action is meant.
The sword image is followed by family division and costly allegiance. The text retains the cross as an execution image.
vocabulary: Apostles
Those sent out with a commission; here the twelve named disciples.
Assarion
A small coin; the saying values the disciples above inexpensive sparrows.

notes: “Has suffered violence” is one reading of biazetai. Another is “advances forcefully.” The identity and role of the forceful people make the whole saying disputed.
The pinned text vindicates wisdom by her deeds, not her children. “Kind” renders chrestos; “easy” or “good” are also possible descriptions of the yoke.
vocabulary: Hades
The realm of the dead, used in contrast with being raised to heaven.
Yoke
A harness image for bearing a load under guidance; it remains joined to learning and rest.

notes: “Something greater” preserves the neuter Greek. The Isaiah quotation follows Matthew’s Greek wording, including justice brought to victory.
The warning about the Spirit is kept in the setting of the accusation about demonic power. The three days and three nights remain exactly stated without a supplied chronology.
This verse is included because it is printed in the pinned Greek text; its variant markers are retained in the source binding.
vocabulary: Bread of the Presence
Sacred bread associated with the sanctuary and priestly use.
Brother, sister, mother
Family terms extended to those who do the Father’s will.

notes: The yields remain a hundred, sixty, and thirty. The mustard seed’s size description belongs to the parable’s scale comparison. The leaven is hidden in three measures, and it affects the whole batch.
Verse 35 says “since the foundation” without the noun world in this pinned text. The explanation distinguishes the world, the field, from the age that reaches its completion.
vocabulary: Darnel
A weed growing among grain; the story stresses the risk of uprooting wheat during separation.
Scribe
A person trained in written teaching, here also trained as a disciple of the kingdom.

notes: Five thousand counts men, with women and children additional. The distance is many stadia; the fourth watch is the final portion of the night.
“It is I” translates ego eimi. The words identify the speaker; possible further resonances are not forced into the translation.
vocabulary: Tetrarch
A ruler of a territorial division; the narrative also calls Herod king in verse 9.
Stadion
An ancient distance unit of roughly 185 meters; the plural is stadia.

notes: The dispute concerns ritual handwashing and defilement, not a medical claim about hygiene. Matthew’s argument returns to unwashed hands in verse 20.
The “little dogs” comparison remains uncomfortable; the diminutive does not erase its hierarchy. The woman answers within that image, and Jesus calls her faith great.
The seven large baskets and four thousand men distinguish this feeding from chapter 14. The pinned destination is Magadan.
vocabulary: Defile
Make ritually or morally unclean, with the meaning developed in Jesus’ explanation.
Canaanite
Matthew’s designation for the woman from the Tyre and Sidon region.

notes: The weather sayings are printed with variant markers in the pinned source and are translated here; the markers are retained in the exact source record.

Peter and rock form a wordplay. Church renders ekklesia, an assembly or gathered community. Binding and releasing remain images; the Greek future-perfect construction can also be rendered “will have been bound/released.”
The saying’s timing is retained without identifying one particular later event as its fulfillment.
vocabulary: Gates of Hades
An image joining the realm of the dead with its gates or power.
Cross
An instrument of execution, used in the call to costly following.

notes: The ancient term literally means moon-struck; “has seizures” describes the reported symptoms. It is not a general equation of a modern medical condition with demons. Verse 20 says little faith.
The pinned Greek source has no verse 21. The established numbering is retained, so the text continues from verse 20 to verse 22.

The two-drachma levy is distinct from the Caesar tribute discussed later. The stater supplies the payment for both Jesus and Peter; the narrative ends with instructions, not an account of catching the fish.
vocabulary: Shelters
Temporary dwellings or tents, proposed for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah.
Stater
A coin here sufficient for two two-drachma payments.

notes: The bodily cutting images are forceful hyperbole about stumbling, not instructions for self-injury. The pinned source omits verse 11; numbering continues from 10 to 12.
“Against you” is printed in the pinned verse 15. Binding and releasing address the disciples in the plural here. “Seventy-seven” can also be understood as seventy times seven.
The immense ten-thousand-talent debt contrasts with a hundred denarii. Family sale, choking, imprisonment, and torture are all retained as elements of the severe parable.
vocabulary: Great millstone
A heavy stone of the kind turned by a donkey, rather than a small hand mill.
Talent
A large weight and monetary unit; the amount in the story is deliberately enormous.

notes: Both the porneia exception and the final clause about marrying a divorced woman are printed in this pinned Greek edition. The scope of porneia is disputed; the draft uses sexual immorality.

The eunuch saying distinguishes birth, human action, and a kingdom-directed choice. Its final category uses stark figurative language for renouncing marriage; it is not an instruction for bodily injury.
Verse 17 asks about the good rather than calling Jesus good. The camel and needle remain a striking image without an invented gate. Wife is included in the pinned verse 29.
vocabulary: Complete
Teleios, also used in 5:48, conveys completeness or maturity.
Renewal
Palingenesia, a new beginning associated here with the Son of Man’s enthronement.

notes: The third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours count through the daylight working period. The last group says no one has hired them.
An evil eye is an image of envy or grudging generosity. The cup language is retained; baptism wording is not printed in these verses of the pinned source.
vocabulary: Denarius
The agreed daily wage in this story; no modern currency equivalent is imposed.
Ransom
A release-price image for giving his life for many; the verse does not name a recipient of payment.

notes: Matthew names both donkey and colt. The final “them” in verse 7 most naturally refers to the garments, but the plural wording is preserved.
The quoted psalm says praise in Matthew’s Greek. The first son refuses then goes in this pinned sequence, and the answer is “the first.”

The people receiving the kingdom are described by producing its fruit, without an ethnic name supplied. The leaders recognize themselves as the parables’ targets. Verse 44 is printed in the pinned source.
vocabulary: Hosanna
A cry derived from a plea for salvation, used here in acclamation.
Cornerstone
The head-of-the-corner stone image expresses the rejected stone’s decisive new place.

notes: The story does not say that wedding clothes had been supplied to the guests. The draft does not invent that explanation for the man’s exclusion.
The Caesar saying leaves both claims in tension. Those raised are compared to angels in the matter under discussion; the text does not say they become angels.
The love command names heart, soul, and mind in Matthew. The psalm quotation places enemies beneath the feet; it is not mechanically conformed to another wording.
vocabulary: Herodians
People associated with Herod’s cause or rule, present with the Pharisees’ disciples.
Raise offspring
The marriage arrangement aims to continue the deceased brother’s family line.

notes: The positive instruction concerning teaching and the criticism of conduct are both retained. The chapter’s sharp polemic is directed at the named opponents within the story, not a license to generalize about all Jews.
The pinned source has no verse 14, so the numbering jumps from 13 to 15. Faithfulness in verse 23 renders pistis in its ethical list with justice and mercy.
The text names Zechariah son of Berechiah; the difficult identification is not silently changed. The hen image is maternal, and “your house” is left without a supplied referent.
vocabulary: Phylacteries
Small containers for scriptural passages worn in religious observance; garment fringes are a separate practice.
Tithe
Give a tenth; the critique concerns neglected weightier matters while retaining the smaller obligation.
